options: The output should stay at 1 while one input changes, but it briefly drops to 0.
The output is stuck at 1 and never changes.
The output should change from 1 to 0 but takes too long.
Two outputs are both 1 at the same time.
items.explanation: The short unwanted pulse is a glitch. A static-0 hazard is the mirror image: a brief 1 when the output should stay 0.

items.prompt: What causes a static hazard in a sum-of-products circuit?
options: Different delays along two paths from the same input (for example one through an inverter), so for a moment neither product term is 1.
Using too many gates.
A supply voltage that is too low.
Inputs that change at exactly the same time.
items.explanation: When the output hands over from one product term to an adjacent one, the old term can switch off before the new one switches on.

items.prompt: F = A·B + A'·C glitches when A changes while B = C = 1. How do you make it hazard-free?
options: Add the consensus term B·C, so a product term stays 1 throughout the change.
Remove the inverter on A.
Swap B and C.
Replace the OR gate with an XOR.
items.explanation: B·C is logically redundant (the consensus theorem), which is why minimisation removes it. Putting it back is the standard hazard fix.

items.prompt: How does a static-1 hazard show up on a Karnaugh map?
options: Two adjacent 1-cells that belong to different groups, with no single group covering both.
A group of 1s that is not a power of two.
A 1-cell in the corner of the map.
A don't care next to a 0.
items.explanation: Moving between those two cells means one input changes and the output hands over between terms. Add a group that covers both.

options: The output should change once but bounces several times (for example 1 → 0 → 1 → 0) before settling.
The output changes while the clock is high.
A hazard that only happens when the chip is hot.
The output never settles.
items.explanation: Dynamic hazards arise in multilevel circuits with three or more paths of different delay. Making every two-level part static-hazard-free removes them.

items.prompt: Which of these are real ways to stop glitches causing trouble?
options: Cover every pair of adjacent 1s with a common product term.
Use synchronous design, so outputs are only sampled by a clock edge after they have settled.
Add extra inverters anywhere in the circuit.
Use only the fastest gates available.
items.explanation: Faster gates still have unequal paths. Extra inverters add delay and can create new hazards.

items.prompt: Why are glitches dangerous in asynchronous circuits but usually harmless in synchronous ones?
options: A clocked register samples only at the edge, after glitches have died away, as long as the clock period covers the worst-case delay.
Synchronous circuits have no inverters.
Asynchronous circuits run at higher voltages.
Glitches never occur in synchronous circuits.
items.explanation: In an asynchronous circuit a glitch on a clock or set/reset line can be taken as a real event. Between clock edges, combinational outputs are allowed to be messy.

items.prompt: In which kind of implementation does a **static-0** hazard arise?
options: Product-of-sums (OR-AND), when the output should stay 0 during an input change.
Sum-of-products only.
Only in circuits with XOR gates.
Only in sequential circuits.
items.explanation: The dual of the SOP case: when the output hands over between adjacent sum terms, both can briefly be 1.

items.prompt: What is the rule for a hazard-free two-level sum-of-products design?
options: Every pair of adjacent 1s in the map (differing in one input) must be covered by at least one common product term.
Every 1 must be covered by exactly one product term.
Use the fewest possible product terms.
Never use an inverter.
items.explanation: Minimal covers sometimes break this rule; hazard-free covers include every prime implicant needed to bridge adjacent 1s.

items.prompt: F = A·B + A'·C with B = C = 1. A falls from 1 to 0. The inverter on A has a delay of 1 ns and every AND and OR gate 2 ns. Roughly how long is the glitch on F?
items.explanation: A·B drops 2 ns after A falls. A'·C rises 1 ns (inverter) + 2 ns (AND) = 3 ns after. The OR sees neither term high for about 1 ns, and passes that gap on as a 1 ns low pulse.
